posts.quote: THE PORCH LIGHT WAS ON, THE SWING WAS CREAKING, AND THE WHOLE STREET KNEW WHO WAS HOME.
posts.caption: Summer evenings belonged to the front porch. The swing had one chain that squeaked in a rhythm you could set a clock by, and the porch light drew every moth in the county. Dad sat with his shoes off and his arm along the back of the swing. Neighbors walked by slow on purpose, so they could wave and say a word or two. Nobody called ahead and nobody needed to, because you could see who was home by who was sitting out.
posts.first: Our porch swing hung from two rusty hooks my father swore would outlast the house. In August he sat out there every night until the mosquitoes won. I can still hear that one squeak.

posts.quote: THE CONSOLE RADIO GLOWED IN THE LIVING ROOM, AND THE WHOLE FAMILY LEANED IN FOR THE NEXT EPISODE.
posts.caption: Before the television took over the living room, the radio did. It was a big wooden cabinet with a glowing dial and a cloth speaker that hummed when it warmed up. Dinner dishes were done early on the nights the favorite program came on. Everybody found a spot, and nobody talked during the story. When the music swelled at the end, you pictured the whole thing in your head better than any picture could show it.
posts.first: Our radio stood against the wall by the piano, and Dad kept a doily on top so nobody set a drink there. We got our evening shows from that dial for years. I still remember the little orange glow it gave off in the dark room.

posts.quote: The smell of rain on a hot sidewalk meant the whole street was about to come outside.
posts.first: We would stand on the porch steps and watch the first drops hit the hot concrete. Then somebody always ran out in their bare feet and the rest of us followed. My mother pretended to scold us from the screen door.

posts.quote: LAYAWAY / A LITTLE DOWN, A LITTLE EACH WEEK, AND THE COAT WAS YOURS BY CHRISTMAS
posts.caption: The coat hung behind the counter with a paper tag pinned to the sleeve. Every Friday Mom walked down with an envelope and handed over a couple of dollars. The clerk wrote it in the book and gave her a nod. Nobody borrowed against what they didn't have, they just paid a little at a time and waited. On Christmas Eve that coat came home in a box with tissue paper, and it felt like it had been earned twice.
posts.first: My mother put a winter coat on layaway for me when I was ten. I walked past the store window every week to make sure it was still there. She never once let on how much she'd given up to pay for it.

posts.quote: DAD CHECKED THE OIL AT EVERY GAS STATION, AND THE ATTENDANT CLEANED THE WINDSHIELD WITHOUT BEING ASKED.
posts.caption: You never pumped your own gas. A man in a pressed uniform and a little cap trotted out the second the bell dinged. He filled the tank, wiped the windshield, and checked the oil without a word about it. Dad leaned out the window to talk about the weather and the road ahead. The kids in the back watched the numbers spin on the pump and waited for the free balloon. Then you pulled away with a clean windshield and a full tank, and everyone had been treated like they mattered.
posts.first: Our station had a bell that rang across the lot every time a car rolled over the hose. The attendant knew my father by name. I used to watch him check the dipstick and wipe it on a red rag.

posts.quote: RECESS / A JUMP ROPE, A KICKBALL, AND A BELL THAT ENDED TOO SOON
posts.caption: The recess bell was the best sound of the whole school day. Doors banged open and a hundred kids poured onto the blacktop. Somebody always had the jump rope, and somebody always had the big red rubber ball. Teams were picked in about forty seconds with very few complaints. Then the bell rang again, and you walked back inside with scraped knees and a grin you couldn't hide.
posts.first: I was always picked last for kickball and I never once cared. The fun of it was being out there at all. The playground had one tall slide that got hot enough to burn your legs in September.

posts.quote: THE COFFEE PERCOLATOR WAS BUBBLING BEFORE ANYONE ELSE WAS UP, AND THAT SOUND MEANT THE DAY HAD STARTED.
posts.caption: Morning began with a sound. A glass bubble on top of the percolator popped and gurgled, and the smell of coffee drifted down the hall. By the time you shuffled into the kitchen, the toast was in and the radio was low. Mom's apron hung on the hook by the stove, ready for the day. The sun came through checkered curtains and landed on the table like it was invited. No alarm clock ever worked as well as that smell.
posts.first: My grandmother's percolator sat on the back burner all morning, and she topped it off every time somebody walked in. I wasn't allowed coffee yet, but I loved the smell more than anything. It meant the house was awake.

posts.quote: A QUARTER AT THE SATURDAY MATINEE BOUGHT A MOVIE, A POPCORN, AND A SEAT NEXT TO YOUR BEST FRIEND.
posts.caption: Saturday afternoon meant the matinee, and you saved your quarter all week. The ticket booth lady slid it back with change in nickels. Inside, the carpet was sticky and the screen was huge. Two cartoons and a serial came before the feature, and the whole room cheered every time the hero got out of trouble. You walked out into the bright afternoon blinking, with salt on your fingers and the story still running in your head.
posts.first: My best friend and I rode our bikes to the matinee every Saturday we could. We always sat six rows from the front so the screen filled everything. I remember the smell of the popcorn the second the doors opened.

posts.quote: GRANDPA'S GARDEN FED THE WHOLE STREET, AND NOBODY EVER LEFT WITHOUT A BAG OF TOMATOES.
posts.caption: Grandpa's garden took up the whole back lot, and he tended it like it was his job. Tomato plants stood in tidy rows tied to stakes with strips of old sheet. By August there was more than any family could eat. He filled paper bags and walked them down the street, one porch at a time. Nobody was allowed to refuse, and nobody tried. You can still taste a sun-warm tomato eaten right off the vine with a little salt.
posts.first: Grandpa grew a hundred feet of tomatoes every year and gave most of them away. He kept a salt shaker in his back pocket so we could eat them in the garden. I never tasted a better one anywhere.

posts.quote: THE PARTY LINE / PICK UP QUIETLY, AND YOU MIGHT LEARN SOMETHING ABOUT THE NEIGHBORS
posts.caption: Some houses shared a telephone line with three other families. Each house had its own ring, two longs and a short, or one long and two shorts. You were supposed to pick up only for your own. Every kid in the county knew somebody else was listening, and you could hear the faint click when they lifted the receiver. Mothers learned to say only what they wanted the whole road to know.
posts.first: Our ring was two shorts and a long, and I knew it better than my own name. My mother always talked a little louder than necessary on that phone. We all knew why.
